review:
The Age of Wonders series has a direct competitor in the Heroes of Might & Magic series. Yes, the budget for the latter has always been higher, giving it an edge in graphics and musical accompaniment. The M&M multiverses have a rich history (most of the lore is tied to Heroes), so AoW cannot compete equally here either. However, in terms of richness and diversity of mechanics, the victory does not go to "Heroes".

In fact, I believe that HoM&M 4 was developed with AoW in mind. I know not everyone likes the fourth part, but I am not among them. Most people disliked the fact that creatures could move independently without heroes, and heroes could die first on the battlefield. This required more focus on micromanagement, which did not appeal to the average player. I will not compare whether this is good or bad because it all depends on implementation.

Age of Wonders 3 proved to be a worthy successor to the previous parts. It managed to retain most of the mechanics while adding new ones. I should note that having all the DLC is essential, as they truly add variety to the gameplay and compensate for the initially limited number of races in the game.

In addition to racial diversity, specializations have appeared, which depend on the leader. This affects the game most radically, changing not only the spellbook but also various bonuses for your empire and granting access to specialized buildings and units (for example, playing as a theocrat, you can get priests even among goblins and orcs). Alignment towards good, evil, or neutrality also changes the set of possible abilities and spells (e.g., the evil summons a fallen angel, the good an archangel, and the neutral a maiden of justice). Together, this provides significant variability in the development of the empire.

As before, not only heroes but also each individual unit (whether a squad or a single character) level up and gain their set of abilities. Monitoring this is interesting, but when there are too many units (especially on a large map), it becomes overwhelming to track where your units are, what they are doing, and where the enemy units are going. There are many parameters for characters (especially for heroes). Not all of them were really necessary (for example, all those "fire," "ice," "dark," "light," "fatal," etc. arrows), but it is still fun to deal with them.

Tactical combat seems unchanged (although ranged units used to miss due to obstacles, now they hit but deal less damage). You can still surround the enemy with multiple armies on the global map and then attack from all sides in the tactical phase.

One of the main features of the game is global spells, where you can change the terrain (freeze rivers, grow forests, dry out soil, etc.), incite rebellion in an enemy city, and transform buildings on the global map.

Neutral cities have appeared, which can be captured by force, bribery, or completing their quests. Some of these cities belong to factions that cannot be played but can be especially useful as they produce unique units (like dragons or giants).

The campaign's storyline is not only interesting but also variable, affecting the playable heroes, maps, and missions. Several endings are a pleasant bonus, and the DLC continues the story.

The game offers many possibilities: building settlements, forts, scout towers, laying roads and bridges, unit camouflage on different terrains (both on the global map and the minimap), dungeon exploration where you can dig horizontally in certain places, diplomacy options (open borders, alliances, exchanges, etc.), a plethora of artifacts for heroes, and the ability to create your own (although they will be simpler). There are many features, and it is in these details that I see AoW's advantage over HoM&M.

However, there is a downside - randomness in combat. In HoM&M, units move in stacks, so the randomness of damage is less noticeable than in AoW. For example, halflings have low health points but have some "luck" allowing them to dodge attacks. This randomness can make or break a battle. The most useful abilities in the game are control (tame, charm, seduce, subdue, etc.). You might get lucky and capture a tier 4 unit (the highest) on the first try, or you might repeatedly fail against a tier 1 weakling.

Verdict: As a continuation of the series, the game has succeeded. I recommend it to those who love turn-based strategies with a lot of micromanagement.

A game with admirable depth, complexity and variety.

I'm a fool for the big map game so that's what I play on and it makes for a LONG playthrough. Wonders III allows you to pick once of several different classes to play (ArchDruid, Warlord, Sorcerer, etc.) and each has it's own unique troop tree. You also have different races, from Draconian to Elves, that provide different strenghts and weaknesses. 

You build your city, draft your armies, explore the map and interact with other AI players for better or for worse. The AI seems predisposed to dislike you, which is kind of nice if you are used to games where it's easy to play "politics" with the AI oppoents through a little gift giving and pocket lining. Takes a bit more to win a friend in Wonders III. 

The armies rank up which means keeping your troops alive and training them up becomes important. If you treat everthing like fodder then you'll fall behind as more "professional" armies start taking the field.

The game has a little bit of everything for the turn-based gamer, the role-player and the city builder. Right up my alley, anyway.

It's difficult to follow up a classic. It always feels like something is lost when a great game from years ago is brought into the modern age. Things get prettier, bigger, and more streamlined, but many times it feels like some essential chemistry is lost. Some of us blame nostalgia, others simply write the developers off as appealing to the largest audience or the lowest common denominator. Sequels always lose something.

Which is why Triumph Studios had no right to produce such a perfect game.

This is the perfect sparkling bouquet of what made the original great, combined with the streamlined production quality we've come to expect from a quality modern game. It's asymmetrical and unfair in the most balanced ways possible. Whether you're outfitting your heroes or designing your player class, you'll find great satisfaction in trying to break the game. You'll be very good at some things, and very bad at others, but it will always make sense and it will always feel right.

The unit design deserves special mention. Each unit is deeply well-crafted and unique, even when comparing racial units of the same role. The attention to synergy is unmatched, both between units of the same race and in the way that race and class combine to make a whole. Leveling up often provides interesting new abilities that also tend to synergize, instead of simply providing better stats.

This game has a lot of everything, and all of it affects everything else. You'll build cities, research and cast spells, and train units. You'll command armies on the beautiful strategic map, and when you explore dungeons or fight another army, you'll go down to fight on equally beautiful tilesets. Tactical combat is reasonably simple but very deep. This game has not been casualized. The A.I. is maddeningly clever, and you won't take this statement seriously until you've experienced it. You'll fight skirmishes in the woods with bandits, and you'll fight in truly massive sieges to conquer cities. Your heroes will explore dungeons, find and equip items, and lead your armies into battle.

You will build your strategy, and then get excited about other strategies you think could work. They probably will. Your race, your class, and your specializations all fundamentally change the way you need to approach the game. It takes a long time to bloom into a full understanding of how the various parts of the game work together, but the journey is pleasant, and you can absorb it by playing.

The campaign probably deserves it's own review. It's gloriously cheesy golden-age high fantasy. The campaign follows branching questlines, so you can end up doing different missions. The base game has two campaigns of eight missions. Eight does not sound like a lot but you can easily spend an entire day playing one mission. They're huge. Think of them more like chapters. The expansion packs can add another two campaigns. 

There are also a number of scenarios which are like competitive missions for X players. The "real" Age of Wonders though is in the procedurally generated random map mode, where you can fight other players or the AI. There are a huge number of random features on the maps, such as "dwellings" where you can purchase units from a non-player faction like Giants or Pixies. You'll need to play many games before you've seen everything you can find. Also of note, Age of Wonders has an underground map, full of caves, tunnels, and the cities of the Goblins and Dwarves.

Triumph is confident enough in the mastery of their game to give the player enormous freedoms to explore how to play. Their own mastery is evident in the careful design of how every element acts together. If you find anything this game does interesting, play it for that reason, but be prepared to fall in love with the rest. 

This is what a strategy game should be. 

10/10

Although Age of Wonders III features story based campaigns and scenarios (many of which are obviously balanced for multi-player), the real meat of the game IMO is the Random Map mode. This is equivalent to the default mode of most 4X games like Civilization, and that's what I'll talk about here.

Unlike most 4X games which start you off with a single settler in a mostly empty undeveloped world, the default mode (normal game flow) of AoW3 starts you off in a populated world which already has roads, cities and armies. In these games you can get stuck into the action quickly and may not need to build any cities at all, just capture existing ones. These games can be a lot quicker to play than other 4X games.

However, the random map games are extremely customisable, much more than Civ. There are three other preset modes - Battle, Empire Building and Adventure - which provide very different game experiences. Better still, go into the advanced setup screens and you can tweak the details to your heart's content. You can start with nothing more than a settler and a leader in a completely empty world, just like Civ, if that's what you want, or you can fill it with as much or as little of the different options that are available. You can also tweak the geography, altering the quantities of different terrain types that will appear on the map.

The graphics are superb, they blow away the old AoW games and are better than most current 4X games IMO. The music is excellent too, one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a game, making it well worth getting the Deluxe version for the 2 hours of music, not to mention the huge 8 player scenario Dragon's Throne.

The huge variety of units in the game, and the many different unit abilities and spells, provide for an awesome variety of strategy and tactics. The game is far more detailed than previous versions, and while the older games were great in their own right, AoW3 takes it to a whole new level. I can't go back to the old games anymore. It's a game you can get sucked into for many, many hours of your life.

The two expansion packs - Golden Realms and Eternal Lords - are real expansions, not shallow cash grabbing DLCs like in many games these days. They add a lot of real content, not just new races and campaigns, but many new rules and game mechanics.

I highly recommend this game, one of the best 4X games ever in my opinion.

This game is absolutely incredible. It stays true to the style and feel of the previous games in the series, while also embracing some of the more modern elements in the 4X genre. Some may find the game a bit "simplistic" compared to other 4x games, but this is misleading. While this game is very easy to learn, and keeps most of the numbers and math pretty simple, there is an incredible amount of strategic depth to this game, and even after over 500 hours played, with 90% of that focusing on just *one* class, I am still learning new things.

The game itself takes place on about 3 different levels. The most prominent level is the tactical combat itself. This is unmatched by any other game in the 4x genre. In truth, it's more akin to the Total War series than anything, except turn based. It is not an understatement to say that this is the best combat system in any of the modern 4x games, bar none.

The second level is strategic movement. Many reviewers and players alike who only play this game for a bit do not understand just how much thought goes into something as simple as moving troops around. Each hex has different movement costs, which affects how fast units can move across them. But the movement costs are variable based on race, unit type itself, and even what the player has researched. Furthermore, different types of units may benefit from terrain features, such as Druids and Rogues who have units with Concealment. This allows some of their units to be rendered invisible in forest tiles. Compounding this issue is how classes and races interact. For instance, Dwarven Rogues are the only combination in the game with access to mountain concealment from the beginning, and this allows for some rather unique strategies involving raiding parties in the early game. While many will say that the tactical combat in this game is what stands out, at the intermediate skill level, the strategic level may actually be more important. After all, you can't actually GET to tactical combat if your enemy utilizes terrain to outrun you, or to reach your cities before your main army can get there to repel them.

The third layer is the empire management layer. This layer is pretty much what your typical 4x player expects to be the bulk of the game, as games like Civ largely ignore the first 2 to focus entirely on management. To those who have played and enjoyed the Civilization series: be warned. Age of Wonders 3 handles city management *vastly* differently than most other 4x games. The key difference lies in how cities work. Unlike civilization, there are no wonders or structures that can be built in cities to give them a specialized role. But don't worry, there absolutely are ways to make cities unique. Where this game differs from most others is that cities are largely defined by the terrain features within their domain. This creates a very different feel to empire management than other 4x games, in that the single most important factor of a city lies in where it is placed. In fact, a city placed on the right structure can often unlock units that cannot be accessed normally, or allow unusual and powerful modifiers to your armies. Some even give massive bonuses to income, or research.

While each layer is important, it is worth noting that this game is still very much different from many other 4x games. The focus is of the game is, at its heart, a wargame. While the diplomacy is functional, the predominant strategy will always be to crush your enemies, and annex their cities. Make no mistake, though. Although the goal is the same in every game, the methods are as variable as your imagination.

I'm not exaggerating when I say that there are players in the multiplayer community who have reputations for using an iconic style or strategy, that is almost entirely their own. The sheer number of options in character creation means that a player could very well run a strategy that is truly unique.

So if you're looking for a fantasy 4x wargame, you will not find a better one out there. Age of Wonders 3 is simply the best at what it does.

My favorite part of AoW3 is its focus on tactical combat while still including all the 4 Xs (explore, expand, exploit, exterminate) plus RPG elements. There are cities to form into an empire, heroes to level up, spells to research, dungeons to loot, resources to manage, etc... On top of it all players are engaged in battles early and often. The battles are killer fun tactical experiences that take place on their own maps separate from the primary strategy map. When a hex is attacked on the strategy map the armies/stacks in that hex and all neighboring hexes get pulled into the tactical battle. This means there could be 42 units (7 hexes x 6 units/hex) in the same battle and they could even belong to several different players! The combat mechanics like attacks of opportunity, flanking, guarding, and 3 action points to use for movement, multiple attacks, or multiple reactions are very well done. When playing single player I almost always choose to fight each battle manually because they are so much fun, but there is an option to automatically resolve them if you wish.

The only bad thing I can say about AoW3 is that it feels like the morale systems need to be flushed out a little more. My wish for morale is that your starting/ruling race should have more influence on the morale of your cities and units and diplomatic relations with independent cities. It was important in past AoW games. These things will probably get improved with some patches, and should not stop anyone from buying the game.

There was a period of years where I played a lot of Civ4 and some Civ5. Eventually I found myself thinking - I wish there was more action in these games and battles were more realistic like... Age of Wonders. Before AoW3 was announced, I searched for recent games with gameplay similar to AoW but nothing seemed to be on the same level. Warlock was too simple and too Civ-y... Total War just didn't draw me in... Others didn't even look worth buying. Age of Wonders seems to fill a special niche that no others do.

edit: Forgot to mention one of the things that makes AoW games so replayable - the races. Past AoW games had at least 12 races, but AoW3 is releasing with 6 which is a little disappointing at first glance. However, this is made up by the new class system which did not exist in previous AoW games. The developers have done an amazing job making both race and class matter. An elven archdruid feels different than a draconian archdruid or an elven warlord. Thus, instead of having simply 12 races to choose from you have 36 race/class combos (6 races x 6 classes). There are also specializations/spheres that further customize your leader and playing experience, similar to previous AoW games. I expect more races to be added in DLC or an expansion and am fine with that.

Age of Wonders III is a 4X turn-based strategy game with RPG elements set in a fantasy style environment. Usually, the game favours wide empires; expanding outwards as aggressively as possible. However, longer and taller games are still possible and enjoyable (but don't do this in the campaigns), just usually reserved for single player or co-op.

++ The setting is fantastic. The game is set in a fantasy world somewhat akin to LOTR, and the graphics still hold up pretty well.
++ Variety of Classes and Races. The base game has six classes and six races; the DLC adds an extra class and three extra races. They all play differently enough, and synergise differently for extra strategic depth.
++ Leader customisation (based on class and race). You can have a lot of fun with it, although it might take a couple of games before you know what specialisations you really want.
++ Map Generation is among the best I have seen across most games. Maps can also have two layers (and more in custom scenarios).
++ Spell casting is a fun mechanic, and fleshed out enough imo. They can easily turn the tide of combat, and provide cool buffs or debuffs to win wars.
+ Music, although preferential. I thought it was well written and different.
+Modding – if one desires more, there are plenty of mods available. Perhaps the best part is that data is stored in a table-format, so no programming knowledge is necessary, only learning where the appropriate data is stored.

- Campaign/Tutorial/Learning Curve: these are all kind of rolled together for the reason that the game is quite hard to learn due to its depth, and the supposed tutorial campaign does little to teach.
- Multiplayer can be unstable; specific network settings are required, and not always guaranteed to work. House rules are normally required as well since the game cannot prevent ‘fast-clicking’.
- Diplomacy (or lack thereof). It’s pretty simple: you can trade cities, items, and gold/mana; if the AI thinks it is stronger than you, it will declare war for no reason at all and become hell-bent on destroying you, or if it is weaker, will try greasing for peace, with not too much in between.

In conclusion, like all games, it really depends what you’re after. I’ve played most of the similar games (like Endless Legend) elsewhere and I think this one is the best. If you are gonna pick this one up, I would also heartily recommend the DLC; they add so much to it.

First of all I'm a huge fan of Age of Wonders Shadow Magic (Aowsm) and Heroes of might and magic 3 (HoMM).

I will compare this game to Aowsm as it should be. Not at ALL. It is actually a 2X: Expansion and extermination as HoMM is (the only difference being that in AoW you can build cities and roads and you select which spell/specialisation you want to have next, but that's it): Fund another player? Crush him. Period. If you get this right, you won't be be disappointed expecting a "Civilization" style game: Get Endless Legend instead.

Let's dig in the core. At first sight, you have the impression the game is a dumbed down version of Aowsm:
- less races
- only surface/undergrounds
- less spells
- no more quest for the gods (this one is really pity...).

You sacrifice this to have the choice of a race + class. And after some hours you realize the game is much better AowSm. Let's be honest AowSm you ended spawning only Karaghs and Death Angels. All other units are useless in comparison with those ones. In Aow3 endgame troops are not overpowered compared to the rest of the units. As such you end up with more diversified armies, like in HoMM. You will build armies well balanced with units from your race and class. Gameplay will differ a lot depending on the combo race/class you selected and it makes the battles much more strategic than AoWSM.

It's according to me the best Heros of might and magic style game ever with HoMM3. If you like this kind of game, this one is a must have.

Just build the big "I WIN" unit and profit.  If this sort of thing does not bother you, this game is worth buying.  Steer clear otherwise.


The Good:

The content of the game is largely solid and well done, if a touch thin compared to other 4X style games.  The game is heavily oriented around tactical, tabletop like combat, with relatively little to do in terms of domestic management when compared to Civilization or the Endless series, or even Paradox's grand strategy games.  If you are the sort of person who thinks playing Venice in Civ V BNW is fun, and are not interested in said tabletop style combat, I imagine you may get bored very quickly.  However, the combat is more interesting than in most 4X games, with a variety of racial unit types fulfilling the standard basic roles (infantry, cavalry, support casters, and ranged units), coupled with class-based units depending on your leader choice and unique racial units.  It is also possible to obtain some neutral units with a variety of other abilities, depending on your circumstances.

In a happy contrast to most 4X games these days, the AI also is surprisingly decent, both in combat and in basic city management.  They will not shock you with their performance, but they are not shockingly bad  either, making solo games quite playable beyond the first exploration or two of the content.

While the developmental playstyle is not much of an option for victory in the sense of Civilization or the Endless series, conversely, city management is simple and straightforward.  You build a city, and its radius of control (and controlled resources) expands with its population and a number of city improvements.  There is no population micromanagement, nor hunting for that one perfect spot - just pick an appropriate terrain type with a reasonable number of resources in its radius and go.

Global spellcasting adds some strategic depth to the game, allowing you to terraform areas to your liking, provide global buffs, improve cities and land, damage cities and land, and provide extra forces through summons, though granted, you often get sufficient resources past the early game that tight management of your spells is not exactly necessary.  

The game is aesthetically well done, and the music is also appropriate and good.  You know what you are playing.


The Bad:

This is a bit of a quibble, but as noted above, you can rather easily run out of things to do other than attempt to smash your neighbor's head in, or stab them, or obliterate them, or so on.  There are two alternate victory methods that are more defensive in nature, but you are not going to win the world over with domestic greatness or diplomatic brilliance (usually).  While the game is oriented around the combat, it would be nice to have a bit more variety in ways to win, e.g. something akin to a strategic game of capture the flag, or some other RP related objectives.  There is at least an allied victory option, though, so you can win with your friends against the damnable opposition, and there are some scenarios with special objectives.

The AI also maphacks.  This is not very fun after awhile, as you can get stretched out while advancing and have to deal with nonsense backdoor attacks because they do not have to scout you at all.  They will relentlessly home in on the points of least resistance and force you to play very, very tediously, as they only do this when your main army cannot possibly get there, which they know, because, you know?  There are far better and less frustrating ways of getting an AI to play with a reasonably sound strategy.  If you must go that route, simply limiting the range of the maphacking or the unit operations script would help considerably.

I found three aspects of combat to be a bit cheeky and nonsensical, as well.  

The first is that ranged flanking rules are highly generous - your unit will turn in response to any attack, and flanking at a range merely requires a bit less than a 90 degree angle to take your shot.  Consequently it is possible to ping pong ranged attacks against a target when both ranged attackers form a mere 90 degree angle with the target (basically a wide cone) and rack up significant extra damage.  This is silly, as practically speaking one merely has to position one's forces in a slight arc or other suitable formation to accomodate for this, as the attackers are still all in front of you at such a distance and angle.

The second is that apparently, medieval siege equipment like rams and trebuchets can be used as active combat units.  Rams can run around impaling your infantry, and trebuchets can apparently move slightly and fire, as if they were a cannon or wheeled catapult.  While they are not cost effective in this role, this is obviously absurd, and allows for some very cheeky rushes of lightly defended positions with barely any true combat units.

Finally, there is no such thing as a proper defensive retreat except for avoiding any damage from the attacker for five straight rounds.  The madness of this design decision becomes comically obvious when a gryphon cannot simply fly away from ground attackers and instead must die, or when infantry engage an obviously faster group of cavalry, and so on.  Having some contingency for this reality of speed and mobility to allow defensive disengagements would be nice, especially given that the game centers around combat.

Tier four units are absurdly strong relative to their cost.  Basic units become an afterthought as soon as those become economically feasible.  Given the theoretical emphasis of the game on tactical combat, this is self-contradictory and not fun, which is the point of games, right?

The Ugly:

This section is the main reason I had first given the game a negative review.

This one aspect of the game drove me to such rage and salt that I actually kneejerk uninstalled the game once.

First of all, do NOT use simultaneous turns unless you are playing with humans only, and even then, probably not, for another reason I will get into.  The reason for this is that, unlike every other 4X I have played that uses this mechanic, there is no delay, no block order, or anything at all in the game to protect you from the AI instantly moving and fucking you over.  This means that a trio of cave spiders, which your adjacent army can easily wreck the faces and burn the corpses of, in combination with the aforementioned AI maphack, will simply charge over to your vulnerable builders and murder them before you can do anything, or an enemy army will ninja attack your city even though your army is also in the same movement range, etc.  Why a pause command or other compensatory mechanics have not been written into the code for this, I have the faintest idea.

Second, the autosave mechanic is relatively bad in this game.  There is no setting for how often you want an autosave, and moreover, it is taken at the end of your turn, rather than the beginning of a new one.  This means that you can fuck up what you were doing at the end of the turn, and then have no recourse, because the game just overwrote your previously good autosave with your fucked up autosave. 

Third, multiplayer is borderline unplayable beyond two or maybe three players, unless you have a very, very patient group.  Ignoring the other problems regarding the AI and simultaneous turns, any combat locks the game for its duration.  There are other established ways of handling problems relating to abusing simultaneous turns, e.g. EL's regional lock,  but the only recourse in this game is to use autocombat.


The Conclusion:

This game is perhaps worth it on discount, especially with simultaneous turns off.

Great game, I bought all of the DLC for it and have not been disappointed. It basically is like Civ 5 but the combat is played out on a small map when to armies meet. Considering the combat is the whole reason why I dislike Civ 5 this was a big boon for me. The game has a wide vareity of races and leader types to play as and has a ton of replayability becasue of it unfortunatley though the larger game (6 to 8 players) can take forever (40 hours) and by the half way point everyone has the highest level units and are basically just spaming them at each other. The AI is very competent in the fact that they don't stupidly start a war with you just because and the roving enemies or bandit camps can actually become a problem if you are play on a higher difficulty (this is a good thing). Really its a great game for anyone who likes turn based games, it is not as deep as Civ is in certain areas such as culture and technology, but it makes up for it well with balanced and fun combat.

What makes Age of Wonders 3 unique compared to other fantasy 4X, and real core of the game are it's turn based tactical battles, there's some serious crunch to them. There are a lot of supporting mechanics, such as spellcasting, flanking, and varying unit types and abilities, but what it all adds up to are tactical battles where you always have interesting choices to make. The battles are fun to watch unfold even after playing for hundreds of hours.

The game comes with two fairly long single player campaigns, a random map generator, and an editor that allows you to make your own maps, scenerios, and campaigns.

Multiplayer works well, but unfortunately the tactical battles can cause things to grind to a halt. I don't recommend trying to play more than a one on one multiplayer game unless you and your opponent have entire days worth of free time. It's unfortunate considering Endless Legend, another fantasy 4x, integrates tactical battles into the strategic layer nicely and supports multiple tactical battles at once, something Age of Wonders 3 can't manage.

AoW3 also has PBEM mode, which I play a lot of. Unfortunately you can't control the player vs player battles in this mode, it's autoresolve only.

Overall this is a great game. I also recommend the two expansion DLC that have been released.

Age of Wonders III is an excellent 4x Strategy Game. I first found this game when looking for a game similar to the late 90's game called "Lords of Magic". Lords of magic was quite similar to this game, but so much was done wrong in that game. The AI was just too simple, once you knew a couple tricks - you could beat it without thought. 

Not so for Age of Wonders, the AI is a good challenge, to me at least. There are a number of classes to pick from as well of a number of skill paths to tailor for your character that will change the play style for any class. The lore and immersion is fantastic, the help/information system is very in-depth and explains any game concept I've had a question about. One thing I really like about this game is the ability to create my own leaders for either the AI or myself and then customize who I'm up against or just let it pick randomly. 

The game seems pretty well balanced overall, although the Necromancer AI leaders can tend to get fairly powerful and be an incessant threat if they get far enough. Although, there are classes and skill paths that can take care of this easily - not every class/skill combination will do well against them. But this game offers a lot of custom settings when creating a new map, so you can just choose not play against AI classes that might be too tough for your level of play or make them all one class, if you so choose. 

This game runs good in a seamless window as well as full screen - so those with mutiple displays will not be disappointed. The mouse automatically constrains to the play area for easy scrolling around the map/battle field - and also handles switching to windows very easily. I don't think this game has ever crashed on me at all, it's stable and runs well.

This is one of my favourite 4X games of this generation (alongside Endless Legend). I particularly like how your faction isn't just a race, but a combinaton of your race and your leader. So all Elves share things in common, and all Rogues share things in common, but playing as an Elf Rogue is different to both an Orc Rogue and an Elf Cleric, for example. Races and leaders each contribute their own units and bonuses and so forth, and learning how to use your favourites and counter unusual combinations is great fun. This extra dimension makes for a ton of variety and flavour.

Everything looks great and the music is pretty good, and the tactical battles where you're winning by the skin of your teeth really shine. Definitely worth getting the two campaign DLCs too, Golden Realms and Eternal Lords.

Easily one of the best 4X games ever made although it does have some annoying quirks, massively OP strategies and occasional clunky interface and mechanics. 

However, it is a wonderful example of asymmetric game design where you play your strengths and counteract your weaknesses. It also has distinct race/culture/magic combinations that force you to branch away from turtle / rush styles.  Another wonderful element is that you can go from doing really well to an actual crushing defeat in a few turns if you over extend or try a risky attack without protecting your capital. It also has make or break battles that will test your tactical ability that can ultimately turn the tide of an entire game. 

On the downside, the AI is a tad weak so cranking up the difficult will be a must although this just stacks up economic bonuses for the AI players rather than better play. The end game can also become a grind so just quit when you absolutely  know that you have won (you will know!) and try another combination. 

The combinations of race, cultures, magic are pretty varied. And replay-ability is further enhanced by the efforts of the modding community that have made this game stand out from a similar pack. For all its faults, it is still a must play for any fan of the genre in a similar vain to Master of Magic series or HoMM. It is showing its age in terms of visuals but great sound track and it is generally pretty stable.  

One major annoyance is that most mods require the DLC so this decade old game ends up pretty pricey... Of course Triumph need to to earn a crust so maybe check it out at the next inevitable Steam sale......

And one final tip... there is a Mod that turns off the Lucky Trait... thank me later!

Age of Wonders III is an charming game but has too much cut and/or unfinished content to recommend, especially to fans of the older titles in this series, both which were filled to the brim with atmosphere.

[u]THE GOOD:[/u]

[b]- Music[/b]
Invigorating tunes that spur you on while you play, great remixes of old tracks while adding in a few new ones as well. Most are of great quality but due to the length of some instances (late-game world map micro-managing or lengthy battle sequences with large armies), the themes can seem to reoccur too often too quickly.

[b]- Gameplay (Leader vurnability)[/b]
While defeat could come easily in Age of Wonder 1 when your leader died to a stray spell, Age of Wonders II made them too persistant with next turn revives and respawning at any city with a Wizard's Tower. Age of wonders 3 perfects this balance by granting the leader some form of revival but at a decent cost. All in all: Leaders are neither vurnable nor near-unkillable like they were in previous games, striking the perfect balance where all tactics can be considered during play to eliminate your opponent.

[u]THE BAD:[/u]

[b]- Graphics[/b]
While city-scapes during sieges can look amazing and army units are decent enough, there are equal as unpolished or plain bad textures as well. The leaders & heroes are the main offenders here: hair, beards and sometimes armor clipping or looking translucent, clothes or armor clipping through mounts,... Customizing your own leader has been expanded upon graphically, which I can only commend but the sore lack of extensive options makes this but a tiny timewaster rather than anything worthwhile. I confess, this is far more important in an RPG than it is in a TBS, but it looks half-assed nonetheless (example: No skin-tone for Dark Elves whilst the High Elves race is a mixture of both Wood Elves & Dark Elves). Furthermore, while some ingame items equipped to these heroes show up on their avatar and thus offers a nice nod to detail, other items do nothing of the sort. In my opinion, either do all or none of the items lest you create the notion you hadn't the time to bother with them all.

Some flying units have issues as well when fighting over lava or water. If the unit in question has an idle stance where it lands itself until ordered, it gets submerged nearly completely in said lava or water. Creating another idle animation when fighting over water or lava could have provided a solution here, as of now it just gnaws at the player's experience.


[b]- Content[/b]
Age of Wonders 1 had 12 playable races, Age of Wonders 2 had 15 playable races (12 in the original, 3 extra in the expansion), Age of Wonders 3 has 6 of these races. Not only a major plunge in what you can play, but all units feel much the same with different skins. Although each races varies slightly from the standard template (Dwarves have 1 extra defense & resistance but cost 10% more gold to recruit, Orcs suffers -1 ranged damage yet gain +1 melee damage, etc...), none feel as diverse as they were in previous games. While some units do have unique abilities (Elf Unicorn Riders pack the Phase-ability, unique to them), their stats are nearly equal apart from their racial modifier! To me, the varied stats seemed to have a far greater impact in previous installments, contributing to each race's unique style. The only units I currently feel that make a unique impact over its peers are the Orc Greatsword and the Elf Gryphon Rider due to enhanced stats or extra abilities.

Next comes the story, spoiler tag inserted:

[spoiler]Even though they try to take the story into a new direction, this game only contains 6 or 7 missions per campaign to explain it. Aside from being utterly uninspired with an ending that just oozes: BUY OUR EXPANSION SINCE THIS RESOLVES NOTHING; all of these missions fall into the same tedious category of: "Build a base from scratch against overwhelming enemy numbers who rarely do anything and sit there until you grind them piece by piece into a pulp." The last and fifth mission of the Elven campaign are notorious for this in my book. Aside from a few skirmishes into your terrain, they'll just wait until you come to besiege them. A few secrets here and there spruce up the lot, but they are far too minor to sit through hours & hours of same old empire building & grinding the foe to a pulp. Since nearly every mission is played with a different leader as well, don't count on transfering your researched spells over into the next scenario like you did in Age of Wonders 2! In my opinion, endless padding. The only plus was that it forced you to play with many of the classes the game has to offer, daring players to test all it has to offer, albeit not that much. [/spoiler]


[b]- Multiplayer[/b]
As many posts on the Age of Wonder III tech support website indicates, a tremendous amount of players is having issues even making a connection to other players. I had this same issue until I disabled my McAfee software, the ONLY game I must do this for in order to play it online even when adding said game to the exceptions list. Even though the game forwards ports automaticly in the hopes to get a connection going for the owner, I still feel this is a nuissance that could have been avoided or handled in a better way than just stating "Your router must cause the issue, call your providers to sort it out!".

When you're finally able to get this mode to work, the only feasible tactic to win the game under an hour is to rush your opponent to oblivion. I've played multiple team sessions and Free-For-Alls, all ended in either two scenario's. A: as stated before, players rushed eachother with their starting stack and hoped to have randomly received a summoning spell at the start of the game in order to crush their foe, quiting if they lost too many units along the way. B: People played passively for an hour and then quit the game due to a lack of intrest. In short: Play with friends so you can extend the game past the hour mark or fight it out until the bitter end. There is nothing satisfying about games ending abruptly because one felt it didn't go his or her way.

[u]VERDICT:[/u]

I wanted this game to be good, I truly wished for this as I am a long-time fan of the series. I adored the previous games but with all the issues & disappointments I've encountered here, I cannot urge others to buy, let alone play it. A few more months to expand the content provided would have made this game a worthy addition but for me in its current state: It falls short.

I've probably missed a few things here & there, but I hope my review helped you decide if this game is worth your time & money.

The third part of a game franchise is often where things are starting to go downhill rapidly, especially if the franchise has been around for a long time (1999) and managed to establish something like a "cult following". The franchise left some big shoes to fill when they released Age of Wonders: Shadow Magic 11 years ago, and Age of Wonders 3 fills them admirably. 

At its core the Age of Wonders series are turn-based strategy games with turn-based strategic battles set in a fantasy world full of fantastic creatures and magic. You pick between different races, create your leader, build an empire and set out to claim the land as your own. You can forge alliances with other leaders (both AI or other players, if you play multiplayer matches) or try to conquer the world on your own. Your leader and hireable heroes are different to your main army in that they can level up and gain a plethora of new abilities and equippable items. Magic is an always-present factor in Age of Wonders. You constantly research new sorceries and in battle you will most often find yourself flinging powerful spells with your heroes while the rest of your army engages in more traditional combat, which also has its own nuances with line-of-sight penalties and flanking mechanics, on top of other things. 


Age of Wonders 3 stays true to the spirit of the previous titles while bringing new features to the table. The most game-changing feature is the introduction of classes. When you start a game you pick a leader, race, class and specialization. Each class gets many dedicated units that are restricted to this class only, for example Arch-druids can get hunters while Mages can summon wisps. The same is true for spells, a Warlord could get a spell that sends an enemy unit into a fit of rage, making it unable to tell friend from foe, while a Rogue might send a plague of brigands upon an enemy city.

Here are some of the features you can expect:

+ 6 playable races, all with their benefits and drawbacks (Draconian, Dwarves, High-Elves, Goblins, Humans, Orcs)
+ Many different spells and units to research, depending on your chosen race, class and specialization
+ Units can level up and gain increased stats, while heroes gain new abilities
+ Neutral cities and dwellings that offer quests and access to unique units and items for your heroes
+ 2 full campaigns serving as a tutorial
+ Random map generator with a plethora of changeable settings to tailor maps to your liking
+ 8 pre-built scenarios of varying sizes with their unique twists, for multiplayer as well as singleplayer
+ Multiplayer with up to 8 players
+ Ships with the same level editor the developers use

If you are into turn-based strategy games you owe it to yourself to at least take a closer look at Age of Wonders 3!

I’ve been playing the Age of Wonder series for years, but I think that Triumph Studios deserve a veritable Roman Bacchanalia for creating Age of Wonders III. It’s proof of what an independent game developer came accomplish with vision, determination, and care for the gaming experience.

The customization options are generous and the game delivers what many games of the 4X adventure fantasy only promise, an infinitely repayable and engaging experience with several modes of play. Personally I like the Adventure mode, for what better fun can be had in a virtual fantasy world then exploring, dispatching monsters, and discovering vast hordes of loot and heroic upgrades? The races are predictable—orcs and frostlings and such—but their weapons and powers are not. I mean, really, what other game out there offers foes who toss exploding chickens at you and gobs of ordure? 

As a “seasoned gamer” of 60+ years, I play games not only for the pleasure they afford but I’m convinced, and there is some seminal research to suggest, that video gaming helps with both cognitive skills and hand-eye coordination. An antidote to Alzheimer’s? Too stiff a claim as yet, but it seems I can always remember minute details of my 13th year after an hour or two in AOW III's expansive realms even if they are details I’d rather forget.

Let’s not overlook the aesthetic qualities of games like Age of Wonders either. The game offers campaigns, scenarios, and random maps that are varied, beautiful, and endlessly surprising. Thank you, Triumph!

To say I like this game would be an understatement. With over five hundred hours on record, and a healthy amount of those hours spent playing multiplayer with members of the Something Awful community, and most if not all the hidden things explored, I still find joy in loading this game up and taking a necromancer out for a spin as I turn the entire world into an open grave. I still find myself impressed by the swathe of modding content, adding more hours to the lifespan of this game.

On that note, it is worth emphasising, [b]Please get the [u]collection[/u] and not just the base game. [/b]Eternal Lords is worth the difference alone, while golden realms is also a really strong expansion. The Delux DLC is a nice bonus but the real prize is Eternal Lords. Necromancers are a very fun class but Tigrans and Frostlings are also great races to play as well. 

Now, lets discuss comparisons. This is not Civ, nor is it Endless Legend. In both of those games, you have a few other ways to win, you can play as an economic powerhouse who wins by driving everyone into a happy friendship circle. This is not how Age of Wonders 3 plays. War is here. War is how you win. 

* Drive your enemies leaders to their knees and take their thrones. 
* Find the seals of power, drive away the guardians and stand upon them, facing rival kingdoms and angry elementals until you master control of the place of power and turn it upon your foes in victory. 
* Unite races together and ignite beacons of unity, driving your enemies mad with envy as you prove your mastery of diplomacy by the sword as well as the tongue. 

You do not win Age of Wonders by becoming king of treasure hill or cutting into other cultures like a knife, You win age of wonders by the sword and the spell. You will lead mighty armies of golems, backed by the might of goblin riflemen. Armies of high elf berserkers, howling furious challenge. Armies of frostling spellcasters, standing alongside summoned beasts. Armies of undead humans, still wielding spiritual fire even while bound to your dreadful will. 

Heroes will be at your command to be equipped by the prizes you rip from ancient tomb and bandit-infested farmstead. From swords to rings to mounts, all waiting to be claimed and lost when your rivals finally kill your promising champion and scatter their prizes to the wind.

You win in Age of Wonders in battle, and battle is what this game does very well. On this note I advise checking youtube for a few videos of the combat. Words don’t really capture it, nor do comparisons. Best to see for yourself.

I'm old enough to have played the first Age of Wonders game, and I wanted to give this one a try. I bought the deluxe set with all the downloadable content.

The creators of this game improved upon the original, not only with the obvious graphics upgrade, but also in nearly every other respect.

The world maps are well thought out, and and the wealth of units with different abilities (with new skills available for veteran units), plus inherent combat conditions and spells, mean a player can't just send a stack willy-nilly into a dungeon or lair. Sometimes a hasty retreat is the best option.

I never imagined I would like the game as much as I have. I'm thoroughly impressed with the designers' attention to detail and faithfulness to the original AoW universe. Although a number of modifications were made, all changes were justified and make sense: for example, individuals from any race are allowed to be good or evil. So it's possible to run across an evil halfling or a good orc.

In the original game, a player would boost up the heroes' mobility, spell-casting abilities, and base stats, and this formula worked across the board, since any character could be improved in this manner and would be an absolute beast toward the end of the campaign, when the hero's stats were maxed out, and this hero could pretty much run around solo and carve a path of destruction. In AoW III, the upgrade characteristics are priced well and allow for multiple strategies to success. It's still possible to "tank" the heroes, but whenever a hero acquires unusual inventory items, new strategies can be enacted that encourage one hero to be very much unlike the next. And this is important, because each scenario is difficult to beat, and following a formulaic script for each hero is probably not the optimal path to victory. And in AoW III, it's unwise to send a hero out solo, even when he or she is buffed out.

The AI is fairly predictable, but in the "hard" setting, the AI is a formidable opponent. I found myself puzzling out narrow victory strategies many times. I dominated only a handful of campaign scenarios, which I chalk up to the hallmark of a great game. I love games where I am forced to think outside the box, and where each battle is essential. Bad decisions early on have consequences later on in a scenario, so laziness is punished. In a campaign, it is usually possible to build up the heroes' stats from scratch, all over again. WOW!

Short review:  If you have any doubts from the trailers and are thinking "Yeah, I want to get this game."  You are probably right and do so immediately.

For a bit more detail:

I'm not even more than 170 turns on a big map,I can already tell you that this is an awesome game.  

At first I thought it was just going to be another 4x clone, which are also great, don't get me wrong, but it's a lot cooler than a lot of games I have played.  

The thing that sets it apart to me is that IT'S DEEP.  And while production and exloration and exploitaing are still the core of the game, there are a LOT of other elements that you REALLY have to consider if you are going to win.  It's much less of a numbers game and a lot more of a strategy game like CHESS.  It is mainly an empire conquest game as well.  There IS diplomacy, but you best be prepared to back that up with force.  It's not really a builder game, but you can totally turtle up if you want to.  If you want to survive in the world you have to maintain your empire.  And thats' before you even meet other players on the max size map.

First off, you have to create your game.  As per most 4x games, there are a ton of options.

There are at least 4 starting modes ranging from nothing but a city builder and a couple of military units, to having a fairly established state with big armies so you can go right to combat if you want!

Next, you get to create your LEADER.  Your leader has a class, and a race. You can completely customize this leader just like an MMO or RPG. There are several classes and several races so that is a lot of options and there are both racial AND class bonuses.  All the classes are "rock paper scissors".  They all have different strengths and weakneeses and they are designed to be equal, if different.  I haven't confirmed how balanced they are yet.  But if you want voral bunny rabbits defending your city, Hobbit Druid has it!  In addition to that, you can style your charcter as you want, create your own flag and colors.  You get to choose 3 major abilities for your leader, such as the power to summon fire elementals out a pool of many!  You feel an imediate connection with the character.

When you get in the game, it's EASY to pick up if you have any experience with a 4x game and even novices can probably figure it out if they click enough things and there are tool tips on everything.  It was very easy for me to pick up.  

The maps are great looking, but the cool part is that there are Volcanic, plagues, frost, and I think a couple of more types of territory and the TERRITORIES are ALSO rock paper scissors for the RACES of your leader and heros, and this factors into the game.  If you send anti volcanic troops into volcanic territory they are going to be far less efficient because moral will be low.  Things matter in this game.  

Another actually cool thing is that there AREN'T these giant research build trees to go through.  You can upgrade a city to max pretty quick in easy mode, which I am playing now in order to get a better handle on the game, but I'm sure the STRATEGY racks up quick.  There are like 3 levels for most abilites.  If you want to park your city and just produce mana you can do that.  Some units can fight on water.  Heroes can and do level up, and units can gain veterancy.

Build cues are kept to a maximum of 5 cue items, either research or unit production.  Yes, it means you will visit your cue more often, but it works in this game because there are less actual cities on the map with an even spread.  There aren't a lot of city upgrades, so you can blow through them pretty quick.  BUT each of them matter a LOT.  You have to research archers if you want archers.  If you want to build a weapn forge (which crafts actual items for your heros) you have to research it first as expected.  There were about maybe 15 unit types under the hobbit units. (give or take).  

Armies are also streamlined because you can only have a maxium of 6 units per army (at least in the game I am playing, not sure if you can change that, but I don't think so.  This is GOOD because you are far less concerned with how BIG your armies are, but WHERE they are and what units are in them!  

Another thing is that each hero or your leader in the game has their own character sheet and as they gain levels you can spend points on any NUMBER of spells and abilities and you actually USE these abilities in combat!  There is ALSO a "diablo like" item page complete with a bag, and character outfitting, and you can send items from one hero to another.   The time it takes to do that is based on the distance of the heroes from each other.  So all the gear AND the spells make this hero or charcter very unique and deployable for specifc roles in an army.

IN addition to that you have a SPELL BOOK which keeps each of the spell abilties of all of your heroes in combat and also GLOBAL spells that you can use to rain fire down units, or convert plague land to fertile forests for example.  You have to SHARE mana between the strategic spells and the close combat spells so it has to be managed wisely!  You learn spells by using research points (candles!) and there are many of them!  You can only cast a certain number of strategic spells per turn, depending on what they are.  

Also, the spells are somewhat dictated by RACE and CLASS!  So the spellbook is different for each game.  But some classes are bad at magic and a lot less effectve with less options.  The Warlord class for example.  But they make up for that with better armor and weapons and archers.

In addition to your basic units that you produce, when you are successful Heros offer to join, and you can have them join you for a one time fee (I think all units have maintence fees, as expected).  Once a hero joins you, they get a character sheet EXACTLY like your Leader's charcater sheet.  Every hero you get is randomized based off race, class, and abilities so they are all UNIQUE.  Sometimes you can win a unit in battle, or a random unit to town will join you.  

The map is filled wtih independants and non-player kingdoms.  They can be hostile or neutral.  If you try and conquer them, some will run but some will fight.  Best be prepared if you want  to win, but stay close enough to your cites or a dragon might blow through and mess up your day!  Sometimes there is an opportunity for them to run, and you can choose between killing them or letting them run.  If you let them run you get good alignment and if you kill them you get evil.  Yes, there are good and evil abilities available when you spec your leader and for your heros.

So basically, between the several terrain types, the rock paper scissors aspect of the heros and leader as well as chaning the compositon of each 6 unit army, you get BAZILLIONS of combinations, and all of the race units are themed for that race like the Hobbit Eagle Rider.  This means just a crazy amount of replayability.

Finally, the COMBAT is VERY cool!  When you zoom in to the battle (IF you choose to manually fight it out) it's an area themed for the place it is.  I went in to one battle zone in a shrine and the objects decorating the shrine created obstacles that had to be worked around in the fight!  Terrain IN the fights is absolutely factors into game play.  Flanking and charging are ALSO part of the game.  If you have a hero on a mount you can charge into an enemy.  Each spellcaster can cast 1 spell per turn, so the combat really revolves around all those abilties you chose for your character.

Anyway, it's all amazing.  If you like strategy games OR RPGS OR 4x genre games, you will very likely like this one.

This game is similar to 4x games like Civilization or Endless Legend except that there's more emphasis on combat and less emphasis on other aspects like commerce, city building, or diplomacy. *Those other aspects still exist in this game but their purpose is mostly to facilitate battles.

The combat is turn based and highly rewards you for good strategic play. Most fights come down to simply having stronger units but even if you have low tier units you can still sometimes win nearly impossible fights with a good mix of strategy and spells.

Individual battles can range from one unit vs one unit to massive wars that can take nearly an hour to complete. If you're impatient (and are sure of victory or defeat) you can also select the auto option which will measure your strength against your opponents and the computer will instantly dictate the winner of the fight. 

 Each class rewards you with unique units and spells and each race also has specific units as well as its own strengths and weaknesses.  Some classes focus on mobility and ranged units, one focuses on spells and summoning, one focuses on resurrecting hoards of undead, one focuses on spying and debuffing, one focuses on healing and buffing, and the other simply conquers as much territory as they can to produce as many units as possible. On top of all that, when you make your hero you're also given a choice of specializations that even further customizes your spell choices and strengths/weaknesses. As you can see, this allows for nearly endless combinations of ways to play the game. They aren't just superficial differences either, each class/race/specialization you play will have dramatic impacts on how you play the game.

You can see how many hours I have in this. It's only going to keep rising. I love this game. It may well be the best strategy game I've ever played. It's heavily combat focused, and that combat never gets old for me. I'm still learning all the time. The highest level AI remains a challenge for me, though that is largely due to its construction; it cheats on the same order as SCII's AI cheats, gaining massive resource bonuses, morale bonuses, etc. It's a challenge, but not a fair one. I still enjoy it!

So, what's it about? War. The entire game is focused around going to war. Do not get it for empire building, there isn't any. The biggest decision you have to make with cities is when it's worthwhile to stop producing units in favor of a building of some sort. All of the buildings either unlock new units, upgrade units produced from the city, increase research output (used to research more WEAPONS), or make the city harder to take. The only victory conditions are war related.

Is that a problem? No. Because the war is so good. The strategic map is for faking out your enemy, destroying their economy, causing their cities to rebel, and striking their armies with spells. The tactical map, entered for battles, is for destroying their armies, and no other purpose. And it is so good. Most of your time will be spent on the tactical map, trying to keep your units alive while inflicting as much damage as possible on the enemy. The tactical AI may be the best I've ever encountered at providing a challenge. You have to be careful, or even the weakest group of enemies can deal serious damage to you. It does have mild flaws, largely centered around valuing damage over keeping its own units alive, in many cases. Which makes it extremely dangerous, if not quite as viable in the long run. Harder difficulty settings easily counter this shortfall by giving it resource bonuses.

Everything has a counter, but no counter is hard. You aren't going to be crushed because your opponent chose a "better" setup at the beginning of the game. You will always be able to find a way around it.

While I myself do not play MP much, the community is alive, both in PBEM and live games, and there are periodic community run tournaments.

In not so brief:
I was really excited about this game. I saw some gameplay and got it on the Steam Winter Sale after waiting forever for the price to drop. I was excited by the combination of strategic overworld combined with tactical combat and thought it would make for dynamic and immersive gameplay. To go with the Civilization comparison I had always wished the combat there was more detailed / more engaging and I thought this was the answer. Unfortunately I fails to live up to expectations.

You choose class and race and those determine what "special units" you get and some specialized bonuses and abilities. Unfortunately, the special units are little more than reskins of the same basic types. You have infantry, calvary, and archers. And your specialized units are only "special" in a few details. Once you get to mid-game you've figured out the most efficient way to conduct your battles in the tactical map and so just rinse-and-repeat through the entire late-game. You end up hitting "auto-combat" more and more because it's no longer exctiting to spend 7 minutes to crush some bandits. And at that ponit you're no longer even playing the tactical portion. Every tactical map is effectively the same, and so each battle progresses the same way.

There is no other choice than "crush all your enemies in combat". While in Civ you can win through economics, diplomacy, or culture, in AoW III it is ONLY through conquest. Well that's fine, right? Because you came to play a fantasy strategic/tactical combat game. That's what I thought. But this affects the AI a LOT. Peace treaties are a joke. The AI will propose them, and then break them only a few turns later. There's no real penalty for doing so and in the end they have no other choice. They HAVE to fight you at some point. So forming alliances in game doesn't really work. As a result, the AI is pumping out units at a high rate. Which just turns the game into an arms race. You don't have time to focus on the unique terraforming spells or anything that's not directly combat related. It's just a sprint to get to late-game units so you can stand up to the AI. Which means you probably get there before even exploring the entire map. So the late game is dominated by just cleaning up the rest of your opponents. Sure, now you have the flexibility to play with terraforming or something, but why bother? The game is almost over.

One final thing is that some of the background game mechanics are broken. Empire Happiness is notably problematic. You gain happiness for a number of things but most importantly for conquering other cities. You lose happiness for such things as losing cities. Happiness determines how well your troops perform in combat. The result of this is that once you get an enemy on their heels it's lights out. It becomes a runaway effect where you just get better and better and they get worse and worse. Instead of long campaigns being tiring for your troops, it's almost invigorating. Additionally, your throne city is EVERYTHING. As in, if you lose that, you lose it all. Literally. Keeping your throne city is a victory requirement. So you can't turtle in a lesser city off to the side to make a brilliant comeback later. If you lose that it's game over. So the easiest way to defeat an opponent is to walk past all of their other cities, go right to their throne, and take it. The end.

I could say more but this review is already overly long. I really, deeply wish I could recommend this game, but it's simply not worth it. Like I said a fantastic concept that falls flat when it comes to execution. If you want to play a turn-based strategy game, play Civ. If you want to play a turn based tactical game, play X-COM. If you want to play a fusion of the two, wait for something better to come along.

Age of Wonders series is akin to that incredibly smart little cousin who gets no attention from the family because the older cousin (Heroes of Might & Magic) makes a lot of money. 

Now, the little cousin grew up and he is... well, considering his age, not *that* smart anymore. But still smart. AoW3 lacks in innovation, but it follows the pattern of AoW2 (which is definitely a plus). Each city you control produces resources according to the features within its borders. You use those resources to construct Buildings inside your city or train Units. With these units you conquer more cities, further expanding the domains of your empire. You also recruit Heroes and train them, as well as your Leader, who can cast powerful Global Enchantments. Every unit has its individual experience bar and level, every city has its own line of production. Think war-focused fantasy-themed Civilization with simplified economy.

There are 9 races to choose from, and 7 classes for your Leader and Heroes. All races share the same core 6 core units (infantry, archer, cavalry, etc) plus 1 exclusive Unit. Each Leader class has its own 7 unique Units, not to mention possible Summons. When the game was released, there was a severe lack in diversity and few combos were worthy but thanks to the devs listening to the community, the bonuses, protections and skills of the Units got adjusted. The races got their own identity now.

I must confess that, although I played all the campaigns, I didn't pay any attention to the storyline. The community seems to be pretty excited about it though, so it must be good! There is voice acting in many languages too, which is nice. The campaigns are very entertaining, however, and relatively challenging (I'm looking at you, Eternal Lords...)

The interface is my main complaint. It feels "minimalistic" but clunky. If your Heroes and Leaders have too many skills, they don't show during combat (you can find them semi-hidden in a menu). The 3D camera and cool visual effects get old quickly, and cannot be fully disabled: you have to skip them at the beginning of every fight. There is no way to permanently speed up Battle Animations, you need to do it once for every battle. You cannot reorder items in the Production Queue in your cities. You'd think that this is a pretty trivial thing to change and that the devs would have taken care of that by now, but we're still waiting... and waiting. Finally, Triumph Studios decided to use a non-standard method for hosting their Multiplayer Games meaning that many players cannot start Online Matches (me being one of them). There are multiple workarounds, some of which involve contacting your ISP - very silly. The mechanics of AoW3, however, don't seem to fit well for Online Matches so I'd recommend everyone to stick to single player anyway.

The Linux port is okay. I've had crashes but my setting is very non-standard. The Achievements were nicely done.

All in all, AoW3 is a pretty good investment. It won't blow your mind if you're familiar with the style. It could use some polishing also but the devs seem to be (sometimes) listening to the community.

This is a really great game for fans of Strategy games who don't enjoy the stress of real-time battles and management. The turn-based system allows for a bit of a more leisurely playstyle. The hero-leveling mechanic and the city-building mechanic form two really fun ways to develop armies and leaders. 

Other reviewers have complained that there's not a lot of strategy in army unit selection, with armies of sheer greater numbers usually trumping smaller ones.  However, I find that this aspect is a nice balance when encountering tougher levels and AI. 

Additionally, the UI and hotkeys make the playing of long turns quite tolerable. 

Another really nice touch is the auto-resolve section of fighting battles. Very Fun!

A welcome addition to the franchise, with some new additions and some drawbacks.

Pros:
+More strategic layers than previous Age of Wonders games with Race/Specialization/Class combinations
+Unique balance of over-world construction, exploration, conquering/destruction, and tactical battles
+Strong RPG elements for a strategy game with Heroes and Leaders' leveling and meaningful choices along the way
+Interesting strategic variety with interaction of terrain and races
+Many and meaningful strategic options/choices in units (skills, abilities, looks, interactions) and cities (city types, upgrades) and empire quests
+Relatively easy to use map editor/maker

Cons:
-Less friendly fire (I enjoyed how friendly fire was handled in previous games) and height advantages
-Less atmosphere than age of wonders games through slightly weaker lore, presence of magic, racial uniqueness, and music/sfx
-Story is a bit weak
-3D Models are a bit ugly
-Less races (Currently) than in other age of wonders games

Differences from other 4x Strategy-Fantasy Games:
-More tactical battle focus
-Less focus on construction

The Future:
The community is strong and kind enough.
The developers are continuously working on the game and listening to the players.
New races and classes are coming out.
New race relations coming out.
New balances and bonuses coming out.
More modding coming out.

Buy or No?
If you are experienced with 4x strategy games... I would get this game.
While the genre probably could use a game to revolutionize it a bit, this game does enough new things to keep your interest if you are captivated by 4x genre.  You may be annoyed with some things here and there, but overall the balance is strong enough and they are working on improving the balance and adding more content to sink your teeth into.

If you are interested in fantasy lore, role-playing/story-making, primarily and racial interactions... I would get it on sale or wait.
Do some research on the game first; if you find the lore interesting, purchase it if you haven't played any game in the genre or wait to see how the updates improve and add to the game in a few months.  Keep in mind you can also create some interesting quests with the map editor/maker.

If you haven't really played much strategy 4x fantasy games and are curious... I would get this game now or on sale.
Your enjoyment of the game will be higher if you have an open-mind and like intricate game systems.

If you are looking for a fast-paced, mind-blowing, competitive game... do not purchase the game or do more research.  The pacing is similar to other strategic games like Civilization.  Also, there is nothing in here that will take your breath away, at least immediately.  The engagement relies on the stories and histories that are created from the complex systems and events that occur.

Overall...
AOW3 is a quality game that could use some improvements.  Fortunately, the developers care so improvements are on the way.  There  isn't too much else in the genre being made at the moment either and is better than its nearest fantasy-strategy competitors.  But feel free to check out games like Warlock, Fallen Enchantress, and Endless Legend as they offer slightly different fare if tactical combat is not entirely for you.

Age of Wonders. I’d say Age of Mixtures. It’s a mix of Civ games meets Warlock – Master of the Arcane with tactical maps of that similar to Fallen Enchantress. You don’t have the fleshed out features compared to your average Civ game, but you don’t have the fast paced combat compared to Warlock either. It fits in the middle with a better campaign than Warlock and the one that doesn’t really exist for Civ.

The combat on the tactical screen goes hand and hand with Fallen Enchantress. You have obstacles to fight past, you can cast spells on your own units or the enemy units, you can flank, AoE damage, etc. Your heroes get to wear items that you can create via forge (certain heroes/campaigns) or finding items throughout the map. 

It fits closer to Warlock on spells being cast on cities, units, or on enemy cities/enemy units, but it drags on and on and on like Civ series. I don’t want to sit there on each map for several hours just to see how the campaign goes and then hoping it turns out to be a decent story; if not, I just wasted many hours of my life.

The AI is a bit off the rails even for medium settings. By this I mean if you’re doing your own thing (I’d like to think Medium AI difficulty is casual with some stings attached) and you come back from exploring and you see four armies with tier four units in it then that isn’t medium settings, that’s called AI spamming the best unit in their arsenal and kicking your ass. 

I don’t want to play Easy but I don’t want to getting spammed on by top tier units as well. Of course, like most 4X games the AI always gets bonuses. Could you do the same? Of course… with negative income, mana, and population and other aspects of your civilization being hindered. 

Honestly, the game isn’t bad and it isn’t great. I’d recommend it being neutral/meh, but since I do enjoy 4X games at times and this wasn’t a bad experience I’d say buy it if you have a niche for another 4X game with a bit more detailed story attached.
